subject: Pathology
summary: Ischemic heart disease (IHD) is myocardial injury caused by an imbalance between coronary oxygen supply and demand, most often due to atherosclerotic plaque rupture and thrombus. It presents as stable angina, unstable angina, or myocardial infarction and can lead to heart failure or sudden death.

sections.p: IHD is defined by myocardial ischemia documented by symptoms, ECG changes, imaging, or biomarkers. Diagnosis requires at least one of these: typical chest pain with exertion, ST‑segment depression/elevation, or elevated troponin.
b: Typical angina: substernal pressure, radiating to arm/jaw, triggered by exertion, relieved by rest or nitrates.
Acute coronary syndrome: new/worsening pain, ECG changes, troponin rise.

t.b: Does the ECG show ischemic changes? ST depression indicates subendocardial ischemia; ST elevation suggests transmural infarction.
Is there myocardial necrosis? Elevated troponin confirms infarction; normal levels make MI unlikely.

t.a: Stress test or coronary CT angiography
t.b: Is there inducible ischemia or obstructive plaque? Positive test supports diagnosis when baseline ECG is non‑diagnostic.

sections.p: Severity is staged by clinical presentation (stable angina, unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI) and by extent of coronary obstruction on angiography (single‑vessel vs multi‑vessel disease).
b: Stable angina: predictable, reversible with rest.
Unstable angina/NSTEMI: pain at rest, dynamic ECG changes, troponin may rise.
STEMI: persistent ST elevation, high troponin, requires urgent reperfusion.

sections.p: Atherosclerosis accounts for >90% of IHD. In low‑resource settings, additional contributors include HIV‑associated vasculopathy, tuberculosis‑related inflammation, and chronic rheumatic heart disease causing coronary emboli.
b: Atherosclerotic plaque rupture → thrombus.
HIV infection → accelerated atherosclerosis.
Tuberculosis pericarditis → coronary compression.
Rheumatic heart disease → embolic coronary occlusion.

sections.p: Patients may have typical angina, atypical chest discomfort, dyspnea, or silent ischemia, especially in diabetics and the elderly.
b: Exertional chest pressure relieved by rest.
Pain at rest or night sweats (unstable).
Shortness of breath, fatigue (heart failure).

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; if a test is unavailable, use the next best alternative.

t.b: Is there wall‑motion abnormality? Regional hypokinesis confirms ischemic territory.
What is the anatomic severity? Visualizes stenosis; guides revascularisation.
Is there myocardial necrosis? Positive result mandates MI protocol.

t.a: If angiography unavailable → stress echo or nuclear perfusion scan
t.b: Does the heart show inducible ischemia? Guides medical vs invasive strategy.

sections.p: Complications arise from ongoing ischemia, infarction, or arrhythmia and can be rapidly fatal.
b: Persistent chest pain >20 min, hypotension, ventricular tachycardia.
Heart failure with pulmonary edema.
Cardiogenic shock, papillary muscle rupture.

sections.p: Treat the underlying atherosclerotic cause, relieve ischemia, and prevent recurrence. Use drug classes with clear rationale; avoid agents that increase bleeding or interact with antiplatelets.
b: Aspirin – irreversible COX‑1 inhibition, prevents platelet aggregation.
P2Y12 inhibitor (clopidogrel) – adds antiplatelet effect, essential after PCI.
Statin – lowers LDL, stabilises plaque, reduces future events.
Beta‑blocker – reduces myocardial O₂ demand by lowering heart rate and contractility.
ACE inhibitor – improves remodeling, lowers blood pressure, beneficial in LV dysfunction.
Nitrates – dilate coronary vessels, relieve angina.
If thrombus present → anticoagulation (heparin) until definitive reperfusion.

sections.p: Long‑term care focuses on risk‑factor modification, medication adherence, and periodic assessment of ischemic burden.
b: Lifestyle: smoking cessation, diet low in saturated fat, regular aerobic exercise.
Control hypertension, diabetes, and dyslipidaemia.
Repeat stress testing or imaging every 1–2 years in high‑risk patients.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic IHD share chest pain or dyspnea but have different pathophysiology.
b: Pericarditis – sharp pain improves when leaning forward.
Pulmonary embolism – pleuritic pain, tachypnea, hemoptysis.
Aortic dissection – tearing pain radiating to back, pulse deficit.

sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring or abnormal, especially in low‑resource settings.
b: Normal ECG early in MI – up to 30 % have no changes initially.
Troponin may be mildly elevated in renal failure; interpret with clinical context.
Stress test false‑negative in multi‑vessel disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain lasting >20 minutes, especially with sweating, nausea, or shortness of breath.
Sudden loss of consciousness or palpitations suggesting arrhythmia.
Rapidly worsening shortness of breath with pink frothy sputum (pulmonary edema).

faq.q: Why does diabetes increase IHD risk?
faq.a: Hyperglycaemia accelerates endothelial dysfunction and plaque formation, and often masks typical chest pain.
Yes; up to 20 % of myocardial infarctions are asymptomatic, especially in diabetics and the elderly.
In STEMI or high‑risk NSTEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset, provided no contraindications exist.

exam: Explain how plaque rupture leads to myocardial infarction and list the key histologic features of an acute coronary thrombus.
Interpret a sample ECG showing ST‑segment depression and correlate it with the likely coronary territory involved.
Outline the step‑wise management of a patient presenting with unstable angina in a setting without immediate PCI capability.
